children: By Kit Norton and Al Root
Investors might be selling shares of SpaceX supplier Applied Aerospace & Defense, but the company is still delivering results.

The aerospace and defense industry supplier saw revenue grow about 49% to $182.1 million in the third quarter ended Sept. 30, while its backlog rose to $1.26 billion at the end of the quarter, up from $1.13 billion at the end of the second quarter.
The company said, excluding acquisitions, revenue grew $24.9 million, or 20%.

Applied Aerospace is a midsize supplier to the aerospace and defense industry, formed in 2025 through the merger of Applied Aerospace Structures and PCX Aerosystems. It builds hardware for space, missiles, and drones.

The company, notably, is a SpaceX supplier, shipping landing hardware for the Falcon 9 rocket. Strong demand in Applied Aerospace's space and launch systems was one of the reasons for the solid quarterly revenue numbers.

That business segment's revenue grew 31% to $39.15 million in the third quarter, and Applied Aerospace said this was primarily due to "increased content on launch vehicle programs amid higher launch cadence."

The largest revenue gain, however, was in the company's advanced sensing and precision strike systems segment. Revenue surged 294% to $48.73 million in the quarter as sales volumes increased across a range of integrated air and missile defense systems.

"Near-term demand is expected to remain supported by missile and munition rearmament, layered missile defense priorities, and continued national defense and budget investments in next-generation precision strike systems," Applied Aerospace said in the earnings release.

It wasn't, however, all good news. The company did revise lower its full-year guidance. Applied Aerospace expects total revenue of between $660 million and $670 million, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, or Ebitda, between $137 million and $142 million. The company previously forecast total revenue between $670 million and $690 million and adjusted Ebitda of $150 million and $155 million.
The new guidance implies fourth-quarter Ebitda of almost $40 million. Wall Street was expecting $50 million.
"Demand is there," said CEO Trip Ferguson on the company's earnings conference call. Material constraints and program delays are impacting margins and timing, he added.
Investors didn't want to hear it. Applied's stock was down 8.4% in early trading at $9.82, while the S&P 500 was up 0.8%.

The drop was also a signal from Wall Street that sentiment around aerospace and defense sector stocks hasn't completely recovered since the midterm election results. which handed control of Congress to Democrats.
It also hasn't been a good stretch for Applied Aerospace stock since its initial public offering in June.

The stock has fallen 44% from the closing price of $19.01 from June 3 — its first day of trading. Barron's also made Applied Aerospace a stock pick on July 22, and shares have declined 38% since then.

Applied shares were trading at about 44 times estimated 2027 earnings then. They trade at 25 times now. Earnings are expected to grow roughly 20% a year for the coming three years, according to FactSet.
The business fundamentals, though, still look strong, and Morgan Stanley analysts last month said in a research note that demand "is intact" across the sector.

That strong demand was one of the reasons why Guggenheim analyst Michael Ciarmoli in September initiated coverage of Applied Aerospace with a Buy rating and $30 price target, representing 180% upside from the closing price of $10.72 from Tuesday.
The average analyst price target for Applied stock is about $23. Seven out of eight, or 88%, of analysts covering the company rate shares Buy.
The company's solid revenue growth in the third quarter was a good sign. Investors still wants more.
